text: A correlation rule like the brute-force detector from Lesson 14 looks solid on paper, but deployed exactly as designed against a real environment, it will almost certainly fire more than expected at first. Real environments are messier than the clean example used to build the rule, and tuning is the process that teaches the rule the difference between genuine attack behavior and ordinary noise.

Tuning usually comes down to two changes. Adjusting thresholds — raising 5 failures in 10 minutes to a tighter 8 failures in 5 minutes, for instance — cuts noise from ordinary lockouts without missing real brute-force attempts, which tend to generate failures much faster than a person fumbling a password. Adding exclusions tells the rule to ignore a specific, already-investigated, confirmed-benign source entirely.

A real, common exclusion case: a backup service account that connects to dozens of servers overnight and occasionally fails a logon against one of them because of an expired credential on just that server. That pattern looks exactly like the rule's trigger condition, but it's completely expected, every night, from that one account — so the SOC adds it to an exclusion list instead of letting the rule keep firing on something already confirmed benign.

Alert fatigue isn't just an inconvenience — it's a genuine security risk. When a rule fires dozens of times a day for the same known-benign account, analysts learn, correctly, that most of its alerts aren't worth a deep investigation. The danger is that habit doesn't turn off selectively: an analyst who has dismissed the same false positive forty times is measurably more likely to give the forty-first alert a quick glance instead of a real look, even on the one night it's an actual attacker instead of the backup job.

Tuning also isn't a one-time task. A rule that's well-tuned today can get noisy again later as a new service account gets deployed or a scheduled task changes timing, so SOCs typically revisit a rule's false-positive rate on a recurring basis rather than tuning it once at launch and leaving it alone.

Next, Lesson 16 covers use-case development: starting from a real risk the organization actually cares about and building the specific detection logic needed to catch it, instead of simply turning on every out-of-the-box rule a SIEM ships with.
